utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is case number IT-98-30/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution. Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour, my name is Christopher Staker. I appear on behalf of the Prosecution with my colleagues Mr. Anthony Carmona, Ms. Norul Rashid, Ms. Helen Brady and our case manager for today is Ms. Susan Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For the appellants. Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Krstan Simic, and I represent Mr. Kvocka in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic is next on the list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Toma Fila, an attorney, and I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. For Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Slobodan Stojanovic, and I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Zigic. I hope there's no misunderstanding on that score, because we have received the documents from the authorised representative of the Registrar. If Your Honour considers it necessary, you will be able to hear from Mr. Zigic himself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll come back to that, Mr. Stojanovic, because there is something of a problem, I think, between you and your client as to where your respective responsibilities lie. For Mr. Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am lawyer Jovan Simic, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this is a Status Conference called in accordance with the provisions of Rule 65 bis. Is there anything the Prosecution seeks to raise in accordance with the Rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Whilst you're there, though, the Prosecution consolidated a Respondent's brief. When will the public version of that be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have given attention to that. We've actually found in practice some difficulty in producing a public redacted version in relation specifically to incidents that are referred to in the judgement itself where reference is made to transcripts dealing with incidents that are described in the judgement. It's sometimes difficult to separate out very precise details that are not mentioned in the judgement from those that are, and we have been exercising our mind as to whether it may be necessary to produce a public redacted version that cuts out individual words in the middle of paragraphs depending on whether it's a precise detail that was in the judgement or not or whether it may be possible to include some of that detail given that the incident is referred to in the judgement anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is a very important thing though, Mr. Staker, that we do have a public version of it. There seems to be almost a conspiracy sometimes between all the parties in these cases to keep everything confidential. I know it's easier, but nevertheless, we are a public Tribunal and we have to have as much as possible -- as much as possible made public. Now, if it comes down to a document that has black pieces across it, so be it. It's important the public have access to it. It's important that the Chamber have access to it so that when we're writing our judgement we know what parts to be cautious about. We don't have easy access to what is given in some sort of closed court or whatever it is and what is not, so we check -- well, we should be checking anything we write against the public redacted version, and if we come across a particular incident in the Prosecution's briefs and we go to the public one, we see that there's a great big black thing, we know to be cautious. At least it guides us what we can and cannot say. So I know there's probably plenty of time but I just want to keep reminding you it has to be done sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can say it is being worked on. There is no conspiracy of silence. We just are wondering whether it may be necessary, in fact, to file a motion seek a lifting of protective measures to the extent that certain details of a non-sensitive nature that are nonetheless subject to protective orders may be mentioned in the public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Anything to avoid another motion, if I may say so. We seem to be absolutely inundated with public motions at this stage, and we would like to avoid it if possible. But anyway, I'll leave it in your hands, but it should be done at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, is there anything that any of the Defence counsel wish to raise concerning the physical condition of their client or the conditions of detention in accordance with the Rule before we get to the details of the preparation for hearing? All right. Well, now, Mr. Stojanovic, you raised this issue about some confusion between you and your client as to who is doing what. I want to make it very clear that you are appearing as his counsel in the appeal against conviction. That includes the motion to admit further evidence or additional evidence. That's part of his appeal, because your client has filed a document as if he were unrepresented in relation to that, and he clearly is not unrepresented in relation to that particular matter. What he sought was an extension of time until he'd got an English translation of the original motion. Now, I'm not going to make that order. Clearly he's not entitled to it because you are appearing for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond, Your Honour, Judge Hunt? I think that you have understood the proceedings and everything that this is about. However, it is a misunderstanding which has emerged from the relationship between myself and my client. My client in fact did not have any intention of doing away with my power of attorney, and he explained this in a motion that he submitted. I'm not sure that you have the translation of that document as it was written and compiled one or two days beforehand. It was a misunderstanding, and he does not wish to revoke my power of attorney. So I wish to apologise to the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I want to make it very clear that that is a matter which has been sorted out between you and him and the Registry, and I understand how the mistake occurred. I'm not concerned about your power of attorney. What I'm concerned about is his application which he filed in person and I've only just received the English translation of it in which he seeks an extension of time in which to respond to the Prosecution's response on the motion to admit further evidence. Now, he's not appearing in person in relation to that motion. You are appearing for him. And his desire to have an extension of time because he doesn't have an English translation of part of the motion is not going to be granted. And it seems to be that there is perhaps a misunderstanding between you and him. He is representing himself only in relation to the appeal from the Registrar's decision to refuse further legal aid. Now, apart from that, everything is in your court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely it, Your Honour. However, over the last 25 days, I have not received any documents because all the documentation was sent to Mr. Zigic. So instead of Zigic, I now need an extension of time. But I would make a minimum request, perhaps only four or five days extension time, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll certainly grant you that. Perhaps you'd better contact the Registry and tell them when it was you last received a document so that everything can be now given to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's unfortunate the Registry is getting itself confused as well as accusing Mr. Zigic of being confused. But there have been matters dealing with that motion for the admission of further evidence which you will have to deal with. The Prosecution objected to material which had been put in reply, an order was made that that be added to the motion, the Prosecution then responded, and there has to be a reply from your client to that further response. I will certainly give you time if you like. You can have another seven days from today. That's almost double what you're entitled to, but I can see that you will have to do a bit of reading. I will make that order later on today if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have received those documents, and I would like to express my gratitude for giving me this extension of time. I think I will succeed within that period of time for fulfilling what is expected of me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before I deal with Mr. Zigic's own matters, Mr. Staker, this question of disclosure. Can you explain to me how the priorities are fixed? Is it only if some Chamber says we want this done more quickly that they get some priority?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a difficult matter of coordination in the sense that it's not the practice of Chambers to indicate the order in which cases will be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, clearly you would be entitled to know whether Krnojelac is going to be heard before this, and that depends upon the speed with which you complete your disclosure. So we don't want exactly to be left in your hands. I mean, this appeal has been standing for a lot longer than Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. The document that was filed by the Prosecution with the status report on disclosure indicated what the respective time frames would be if this case were dealt with before the Krnojelac case or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, only to the extent that they said they wouldn't be finished until April of next year, which is a very grim prospect. But it then goes on to discuss that in the absence of any further order, that is the situation. But if we said, "Look, these people have been in custody for a very long time. It's a long time since the decision was given, much longer than since the Krnojelac decision. What would be the prospects of getting it earlier than April of next year"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the reality is that the Office of the Prosecution has a given number of resources. If further resources were devoted to this case, that would mean less resources and corresponding delays in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's matter for the Office of the Prosecution to work out how it allocates the resources which it has. You see, from the Appeals Chamber's point of view, if this matter is not ready because of the delay in disclosure, then they will list Krnojelac, because they say they must get on with their conviction appeals. But it seems to me that Krnojelac is going to take priority over these appellants simply because it's going to be easier to do the Rule 68 disclosure for him than it is for these, and there seems to be some sort of imbalance there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I think all I can say, Your Honour, is that our filing has explained the situation, and beyond that, we're in the hands of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, the most helpful thing that Mr. Blewitt's submission has done is to tell me what the name is for those accents on the letters. They're called diacritics, apparently. I often wondered what they're called. But apart from a that he's left it up in the air. He says they won't be ready until April if he keeps the same resources on it now that are presently on it. We think that there's a time, especially for an appeal, that there should be some diversion of other resources to get this one ready. Understanding all the problems about doing these Rule 68 searches during the course of a trial, nevertheless there is an obligation on the Prosecution to keep going on Rule 68 even after the trial. And it seems to me that that obligation has to be looked at in accordance with the priority given to the cases in the ordinary course, and the ordinary course is this case has got priority over Krnojelac. But if we are met with the statement that you won't be ready until April 2003, well, then the Appeals Chamber will simply list Krnojelac first, and that seems to be unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should also indicate, I think this is clear from the filing, that it is the same resources that are working on this case that would work on the Krnojelac case and that on the current scheduling -- on the current scheduling, that is why the one case would be dealt with after the other has been finished, and that if more resources were to be given that would the be expense not of the Krnojelac case but of some other case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it may be that that will have to be done. We're not here to tell the Prosecution how to order its resources, but are here to say, "We've got to get on with this appeal." And if Rule 68 hasn't been complied with, well then, it is unfortunate, but the Prosecution does have an obligation and it has to order its priorities not just to this little team that you have doing Rule 68 material. I think we said somewhere in the decision that Rule 68 is just an important an obligation as getting an indictment in and giving the material which you rely upon to support the indictment, and it seems to mean something which unfortunately has been put to one side as to be done when possible. Now, it may be just a matter of terminology, but in paragraphs 11 and 12 of Mr. Blewitt's document I read it, I hope wrongly, as saying that you'll wait until you've got all the material before you start work on it. In each case in the last sentence: "Within six weeks of receiving the last of the documents" and again, "within two months of receiving the last of the documents," or is it going to take two months to check the last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Well, the document says it will take up to two months to check up to the last of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why? Why isn't the work being done as it comes in?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't understand what's intended by those two paragraphs or the last sentence in each of them. If you said it's going to take -- the amount of material that has already come up on the initial check-through such that it's going to take us five months or six months or eight months to check it all, I can understand it, but that's not the way it reads. It reads as if you are going to wait until the last document comes in and you're going to then start checking it, whereas, I can't imagine it would take two months to check a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the documents are being looked at as they're received by the Appeal Section from the ISU. Nonetheless, it's not the case that the documents necessarily come on a day-by-day basis but in batches, and time is required to review and in some cases to deal with translations or other verification or checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, what is it you feel that is the way around this, that we just order that it be given expedition?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the same resources are also doing the disclosure searches for other appeals cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Who is doing the ones for the Trial Chambers?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: It's the same ISU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Well, don't you think that with the problems that we've been having about Rule 68, and they have accumulated massively over the last four years since I've been here, that some more resources should be given to that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a matter that goes beyond my brief in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know, but I'm wondering what we can do to impress upon the Office of the Prosecutor that it's not just sufficient to say, "Well, we only have 15 or 25 or whatever it is people to do this." They've got to pull their resources from somewhere else to assist them because it is vital to have this material disclosed, and I know that the orders I've been making occasionally on the seizure of documents are not exactly popular upstairs, but it's because of the failure to do this in the first place that most of our problems about disclosure have occurred. I'm talking about the Appeals Chamber's point of view, that matters are found in the Office of the Prosecutor for the first time after the judgement has been given by the Trial Chamber, and despite every endeavour that we have made over the years to try and improve it, nothing seems to be happening to improve that situation. Now, it's not for me to make that such an order, but I think it's something which the Appeals Chamber is going to have to consider, because at the moment, as I say, they will list Krnojelac, I'm not in it of course, but they will list Krnojelac if this case is not ready, and they will do it regardless of what your resources are, because the Appeals Chamber is going to get very much further behind if it can't get some of these appeals out of the way. Well, is there anything more you want to add about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there's anything I can add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We all have problems with resources. The Chamber's area of this Tribunal are probably given the least resources of anybody, and we've tried to do our best with what we've got. It's about time, if I may say so, the Office of the Prosecutor faced up to the same situation. Anyway, I'll talk to the rest of the Trial Chamber and see what we propose to do, but if we make an order that expedition be given to it and that's what Mr. Blewitt's document suggests has been done in some cases, then you will be ready for it. All right. Well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zigic, I want to speak to you, if I may, about your appeal against the Registrar's decision. I want you to understand that you are not just entitled to have access to all of the Registrar's documents. It's what's called a fishing expedition, and I'm sure you understand what I mean. You can't go in there looking to see if there is something which will assist you. You have to demonstrate some reason for getting the material from the Registrar. Now, you did that very well when you said what you wanted -- the last time when you said what you wanted to prove was that you had made complaints to the Registry about the conduct of one of your counsel, and that led them to concede that they would provide the material to you and a whole series of memoranda or extracts from memoranda where you had made what could be interpreted as complaints about one of your counsel, they have been now disclosed to you and to us. But you can't just say, "I want everything." If there's something else you want to establish in your appeal, you have to nominate it. And please do not send your documents to me. They must be filed with the Registry. That's the only way in which everybody will get a copy. So may I suggest that if there is something more you want from the Registry files, you nominate what it is you want to prove and then the Registry will consider whether they should disclose it. If they say they won't, then we'll consider whether we order them to do so. But we want you to do the same as you did when you got those documents. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT ZIGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have understood you fully. Thank you for giving me this opportunity to address you regarding this problem. Thank you very much for the suggestion that you have just given me. I have fully understood it. On the 24th of October, I spoke with the Deputy Registrar regarding my problems and regarding my latest motion requiring that the transcripts from the meeting be disclosed to me. I received transcripts that I didn't ask for. I received some other ones, and I clarified that with the representative of the Registry. I have to now give him a very specific list of the dates for transcripts that I'm interested in, and he promised to reply favourably regarding that. Now I have to solve the problem with Mr. Stojanovic who is my attorney representing me in the appeals case, in the appeal against my conviction, and I would now like to apologise to you for the enormous number of motions I sent to you. I know that your time is very valuable, and I hereby promise to you this will not happen again in the future because I now have an attorney representing me. As far as the appeals motion filed on the 8th of July is concerned, Your Honour, I would like to tell you that right now I'm representing myself. If the Chamber should rule that there is a proceeding going on to this effect, I will have to retain an attorney, and I'm not sure who is going to pay for that. Regardless of whether the Registry will agree to pay for my counsel, I will have to have one, because it is obvious that I will not be able to represent myself in the future. Things that I have done so far I did on my own, and the time will tell what the quality of that work is. At any rate, Your Honour, thank you so much for giving me this opportunity to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't have the papers here with me, Mr. Zigic, but is the motion that you referred to, the one of the 8th of July, is that the appeal against the Registrar's decision?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT ZIGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision of the Registry was rendered on the 8th of July, the decision to refuse any further legal aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you saying that you're not going to appear unrepresented in relation to that appeal? Because the Registrar has refused to give you any legal representation for that. What is it you want to do about that?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT ZIGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was informed by Mr. Christian Rohde that there will not be a proceedings instigated regarding this but, rather, an administrative procedure. So there will be no need for me to have a legal counsel. I only said that should there be any proceedings instigated in addition to this administrative procedure, then in that case I will need to have a legal counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be just a question of terminology, but it is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not administrative the way in which your appeal against the Registrar's decision of the 8th of July will proceed will be on the written material which is provided. There won't be a hearing as there is here today. The Judges won't come into court and you will be expected to address us on the matter. It is going to be decided, as I understand it, on the written submissions that are made. So that's may be what Mr. Rohde is referring to. But you are still going to put your submissions in in person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT ZIGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But right now at this moment, I don't have any instruction to file any motion. Should you in the future put in such an instruction for me to file any submission or a motion, then I will do that on my own without an attorney. And in order to facilitate the situation for you, Your Honour, I'm sure that what you said is correct. And if there is not going to be a typical procedure, a typical hearing with witnesses and so on, and if the decision is indeed to be rendered based on written material only, then I believe that I will have no need to have somebody represent me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The only thing that you will have to do is to file a reply to the Registrar's response. Now, that haven't been filed yet, and they've been told to get on with it. They will file their response to your appeal and then there will be a translation made of their response and that will be given to you, and you will then be required to file your reply to that. Now, that is something which I haven't spoke to anybody, but I understand will be filed this week as their response. It will obviously take some time to be translated for you, but then once that is done, we will make an order that you file a reply. I had in mind seven days after you receive the B/C/S version of it. So you've got plenty of time. I'll see how big it is. If it is bigger I'll give you more time. Usually you only get four days, but I thought seven would be fair because you are doing it without the assistance of a lawyer. But that's a matter you have yet to do. You can't do it until you've got the B/C/S version of their response. After that, it will be simply a matter for the Appeals Chamber to consider your appeal against the Registrar's decision. So then we need not concern ourselves, need we, about you wanting further representation for that appeal? That's the appeal against the Registrar's decision.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT ZIGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're fully correct, Your Honour. I will not be using the services of a legal counsel in response to the reply by the Registry. Thank you for extending the deadline for me. And may I ask this as well: If the response by the Registry is voluminous, then I would ask you for additional time to respond to that. My resources are quite limited. I don't have the entire documentation in my quarters, and maybe I will have to get additional information and certainly additional time will be needed for that. So it all depends on how large the motion filed by Registry is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that, and I will certainly listen to anything you want to say. When it comes in, I will make an order. I will try and assess it myself. If you believe it's not enough, it's open to you to make an application for further time. But you must remember that the more time that's being taken with this appeal, the later the hearing of the appeal against conviction which we are trying very hard to avoid any further delay there, as you may have gathered with my conversation with the counsel for the Prosecution, but thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT ZIGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, is there anything else which the parties wish to raise? Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to go back, with your permission, to the problem of disclosure, because I wasn't able to make a comment with respect to the motion of the Prosecution because you asked Mr. Zigic to state his views. So I'd like to go back to something that is very sensitive in this case and these proceedings. May I, with your permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are concerned with the motion and its contents, especially as we're faced with a quite specific situation whereby today we have two accused who, in keeping with the Tribunal's practice, should be released in a short space of time. Mr. Kvocka, on the 9th of December, will have been in prison for six months, and the practice has been that they should be set free after that. And Mr. Prcac is arriving -- has come to that date. I hope that these proceedings will not go on for too long until they complete their sentence, because in one of the paragraphs is says that 292 days are necessary plus 971 which makes it a total of about three years. We're also very concerned about the fact that these documents should have been disclosed during the course of the trial itself. We're now faced with a situation when we have launched our appeal, and we have received a response from the Prosecutor mentioning some 1.000 documents, and this is a difficult situation for us. But the best situation for us, the most favourable would be if you were to set a date for oral argument, and might I be allowed to state that the Krnojelac case and Kvocka case have been ranked. There seem to be different questions, different issues at stake. I'm afraid this might be a part of a strategy to have the Krnojelac case dealt with before the Kvocka case for certain positions and stands which would be to the detriment of our clients, not only from the appeals side but also the time they would have to wait. And I'd like to refer to Article 21 of the Statute which does require all participants in the proceedings to ensure a fair and efficacious trial, a speedy trial for the accused. And also Article 11 of the Convention of Human Rights and Freedoms also guaranteeing a speedy trial. I am afraid that in this stage of the proceedings we would have to wait for all this time and from the aspects of Mr. Kvocka, this would serve no purpose. It would not be to our advantage. We are ready now to give up the benefits that can be given to us with the disclosure of documents because they cannot bring anything substantially new. The case is over. The Prosecution did not make an appeal. All that remains to be done is to hear the judgement of the Appeals Chamber and the wording of that. So we do really feel that this is no easy problem, of course. It is one that requires due consideration, because we are dealing with accused here who have been in detention for five years and that period of time is being extended, and we must start out from the indictments and the charges and what it all boils down to. After that we once again have April as a time limit for getting through all the deliberations, which means that I won't be able before next autumn to complete this process. That is why I should like to ask you and appeal to be, because this is a very great problem for us, and that a date be set and that we show respect for this time period for the final presentations. You said that this could be sometime at the beginning of November. Could you please reconsider and look at the position of the accused. Mr. Kvocka is in have very difficult position. The 9th of December was the date when he was to go home, but he has to stay and wait for documents that ought to have been disclosed during the trial itself if he is to be given a fair trial and the right to a fair trial accorded. So this is a serious problem for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Simic, may I deal with it perhaps in the same order that you have. You say that the documents which the Prosecution will be producing will have nothing substantially new in them. If that is your belief and that is the belief of all of the appellants, then the Prosecution need not proceed with it. As you point out, they are not putting them forward in support of some appeal of the Prosecution. They're putting them forward as part of their obligation to disclose to you material which may be exculpatory. So that if you feel that there is going to be nothing exculpatory in all of these documents which the Prosecution are searching through, then say so, the lot of you. If you say so, we will tell the Prosecution to forget Rule 68 and we'll get on with the hearing of the appeal. If I were you, I would not do so because it's surprising that in most of the appeals so far the material which the Prosecution is now finding is indeed exculpatory in nature. Now that's a matter for you. There's nothing that requires the appellants in this case to wait for the Prosecution to disclose the material which they should have disclosed earlier under Rule 68. But generally, if I may say so, appellants say, "We want to see what there is which is exculpatory because if it's there we want to rely upon it in our appeal." So that's the first point I want to make. The second one you say according to the ordinary practice of this Tribunal, your client would be free to go home on the 9th of December. Now you would have received the decision of the Appeals Chamber refusing provisional release and you, if you want to establish some particular ordinary procedure or usual rule, you try, but there is no such usual rule. When somebody is going to be released, it depends upon the identity of the country to which he is sent to serve his sentence because all countries have different remissions assistance. So there is no basis for your client to believe he is entitled to go home on the 9th of December. And if you want to go off and serve your sentence and you are lucky enough to get a country that does have a very large remission system, then it's a matter for you. You can go off and do it and be released on the 9th of December. But don't come here and saying your client is being denied his right to release on the 9th of December because that just isn't so. Now, the next thing you said was that there was going to be three years involved in the Rule 68 disclosure. I'm afraid you've fallen for the easy trap that the Prosecution appears to be setting in these cases of referring to the number of days it will take if one person does the exercise so that if it's going to be 700 hours, it will take one person to do it, and then if they put on ten people, it's only going to take 70 hours. And we've got some information in Mr. Blewitt's documents as to the number of people they have on this particular exercise. How that extends to April 2003, I'm not sure, but it's no good relying upon the amount of time which they say this is going to take or the number of days it's going to take. That's only if one person is handling it at a time. So the more people they put on, of course the less time it will take. So I understand your client's concern about the time this is taking, and it's a concern we have expressed on several occasions in the Appeals Chamber that these appeals are being delayed because of the problems the Prosecution is having with disclosure. And I think you might have gathered from what I said to Mr. Staker that we're not very happy with the way in which we are being presented with these delays. So you need not concern yourself that we are very anxious to get on with this appeal ourselves. But we are not going to proceed upon the basis that your client has some right to be released on the 9th of December. He doesn't. Now, is there anything more you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one sentence. I don't think you understood me. I think that -- I said that it was the practice so far and that the Tribunal released two people from the Detention Unit and didn't send them on for further -- a further period in detention after they had served two-thirds of their sentence, because after they have -- I don't want to mention half the sentence that they have served. They were amnestied afterward. But I will give up my right to Rule 68 so that I could get a decision from the Appeals Chamber as fast as possible. So I'm fully conscious of the fact that these documents could have something among them which would be to my advantage, but I give that advantage up because I should like to hear the stand of the Appeals Chamber as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you persuade all of your colleagues to do so and your clients are fully informed of what they're giving up and they put in writing that they do, then we'll consider listing the appeal. But at the moment, we would not do so unless all appellants gave up their rights under Rule 68, which I can't imagine them doing if they're being properly advised, and that we have something in writing from them saying that they have been properly advised and notwithstanding the fact that in many other cases exculpatory material has been produced as a result of these searches but they don't want to hear about it, that's a matter for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, does anybody else want to add anything to that? Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the subject of my concern is what concerns you and Mr. Simic both, that is to say the length and time all this lasts and how Rule 68 can be applied. In the course of the proceedings, I knew that those documents were with the Prosecution, that the OTP had them, and the Defence of Mr. Prcac and myself asked to see those documents because they are documents in the Serbian language. You will be able to see that my investigator, Mr. Takic from Prijedor, and Dusan Masic as well, legal advisor, co-counsel, in fact, of Mr. Simic, they were given the opportunity to see those documents, and we looked at them for ten days. Take a look at the transcript and you will find in it that we were able to see those documents. But when we asked that all the documents be provided us, the Prosecution refused and said that that was impossible. All this can be found in the transcript from the trials. I haven't got the transcript with me now, but we have four binders full of them, and I can show you them now if you like. But what Mr. Simic is concerned about and what you are concerned about yourself, Your Honour, and I myself too, is why suddenly we are being offered this now when beforehand when we asked to be disclosed these documents we weren't given them. We were refused. And I'm talking to the documents before the final argument on the 29th of July last year. From Mr. Blewitt's letter, it appears that they had received these additional materials two days prior to that, and they failed to inform us about this earlier on, before the closing arguments. They failed to tell us that they had these documents before the closing arguments and did not allow us awhile to take a look at them and then go ahead. So why are we concerned? We're concerned because we feel that there is something else that this is masking. If it is the desire to do with the Krnojelac trial first because there's something they don't like there, to deal with that trial first, but quite obviously the judgement is something that the Prosecution does not seem to like. So I am concerned about the order. I don't want the order upset. I don't want the Prosecution to bring the Appeals Chamber into a position to look at the Krnojelac appeal first and then our own later on. All these documents are in the Serbian language. There is no need for them to be translated. You can provide them to us within a space of 30 days for us to take a look at them, and we can select what we need from all those documents, those that we feel to be exculpatory material. It's not in English, and therefore does not have to be translated into Serbian. It is vice versa. So what we would like the Prosecution to do is to give us those documents in the B/C/S language within a space of seven days, and we will be able to assess whether this material is exculpatory or not, whether it tells us something or not. We know that there is something that might be useful to us. Perhaps not. But nevertheless, it is our concern with respect to the length of this trial and these proceedings, and I can't understand why it was necessary to have 15 or 16 months from the moment they received these documents that suddenly now they have taken it into their minds to disclose it pursuant to Rule 68, whereas they had no desire to do it previously. So that is the concern which we here feel and which Mr. Simic presented and that it probably has something to do with the Krnojelac trial, to have it resolved in a way that is different to the way in which it has been resolved already. And that is why we propose that you order the Prosecution to supply us with the documents that it has in its possession within a space of seven days. We can look through the documents and then have another meeting to say whether we need any of them or not. Let me make things quite clear. We do not need any B/C/S documents to be translated into English and back into Serbian again so that we can read in the B/C/S language whether we need them or not. If it is in the interests of the Prosecution to help us, and I don't really believe that to be the case but I would like it to be, then there's no need to do that and there's no need for Mr. Blewitt to be concerned. Give us all the documents you have and we'll see for ourselves. So you don't have to help us settle our own problems. We will do that ourselves. That's what I wanted to say, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Staker, what Mr. Fila says is something worth considering if I may suggest it. I'm not suggesting that there's some plot by the Prosecution to delay this appeal until after Krnojelac. I know the issue between the Krnojelac judgement and this one where we disagreed with something that had been said in this judgement, but I'm not suggesting that's a matter that I need to concern myself with here. But the suggestion he makes is why do you need to go through the process if you've got this material and these names come up, does it matter if you disclose too much and let them look at it without waiting for it to be indexed and paginated and all the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a question of the general structure of the Rules. Rule 68 requires disclosure of exculpatory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I realise that. I realise Rule 68 requires that, but why don't we treat it, in effect, like an application by them to have access to this material? What is the problem with it? It would be so much faster than having to wait until next April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: With Your Honour's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I should add I don't expect you to give a final statement now, but is there not something worth considering in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to say if I could take that question on notice. I understand there are issues relating to identifying Rule 70 and issue relating to identifying material and may be subject to protective measures in other cases that would require --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that when you are giving this some consideration that you follow what we did in Brdjanin and Talic where this similar sort of issue arose? Rule 70 material, certainly that has to be identified, but if you provided everything redacted as to identification and wait until you hear from the appellants whether they particularly want to know the identity of the witnesses whose statements they've been given or whose evidence they've been given before the identity of anybody is disclosed and you deal with it as an application for access to this material, it overcomes all of these problems about Rule 68. I think that most of us understand that the logistical problems which the Prosecution has in relation to Rule 68, but that's not a reason for ignoring it, which I sometimes think Rule 68 is put on the back burner upstairs. But in this case, it seems to me that these people have been in custody for a very long time, and it is a case which should be given priority over Krnojelac. Now, I know the issue about persecution is a fascinating one and that you will all want to get Krnojelac upset, but I don't think we should try to juggle cases, in case this is in anybody's mind, in order just to suit the Prosecution's strategies as it was put. I'm not suggesting there is one, but I hope -- and I hope that there isn't one, but we really must get these appeals off the ground, and next April is not soon enough. Now, when do you think you might be able to come up with some sort of response to what Mr. Fila has suggested?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: If we could request a week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Well, the best thing to do would be if you could file something by, say, next Tuesday, and then we can have a look at it, and there will be an opportunity for the appellants to respond to it. But it seems to me, with all due respect, a very simple way out of your logistical problems that Rule 68 gives rise to, provided that Rule 70 material can be easily identified and that the identity of people is redacted until it can be shown that it is of some use, the material is of some use to the appellants. But perhaps if you need more time let me know, but I think we have to put a time limit on it, and I suggest at this stage by next Tuesday, which will be the 5th, 5th of November. Right. Well, now, does anybody else want to -- I'm sorry. Mr. Fila, you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Just to make ourselves understood, Your Honour. The first batch of material I have had a look at. They are papers that have been amassed from the Prijedor Police Station and Omarska too, one or two trucks. There's nothing there that would come under Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that means it will be easy for them, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, does anybody else want to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, then. Well, we look forward -- yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you've already solved the question. I should just like to emphasise that we should join in this request to have these materials looked at And what Mr. Blewitt mentions. Our case is a very serious one, and it would be a very bad idea to miss this opportunity. And the Zigic case is tied to a lot of incidents and events, a lot of documents are being offered, and we should like to come out in support of this proposal fully that we be supplied with all the documents and material. Thank you so much from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, what I suggest happen is that after the Prosecution has filed this response to Mr. Fila's suggestion, that you, as soon as possible, file your own response to that so that we know where we are, and I can consult my colleagues in the Appeals Chamber as to what attitude we should take towards it. I only say that I think it was a good idea. I'm not suggesting that it's something which we're going to necessarily override any objection from the Prosecution, but it is something which is worthwhile considering in order to block this terrible, terrible procedural problem with Rule 68. Well, thank you all for coming, and I will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: at 4.58 p.m.
